Molecular docking against Plasmodium falciparum dihydrofolate reductase-thymidylate synthase (PfDHFR-TS) was performed to investigate potential ligand-target interactions. Drug loading and HCQ release were evaluated at pH 7.4. We also assessed in vitro cytocompatibility, nitric oxide estimation, total antioxidant capacity, anti-inflammatory and antimalarial activities. Results: The physicochemical characterization supported the successful formation of HCQ-ZnONPs. In the proposed model of HCQ-ZnONPs, a quinoline nitrogen of the HCQ molecule interacts with an exposed Zn2+ site on the surface of a ZnONPs cluster. The HCQ-ZnONPs exhibited a drug loading of 21.4% and showed approximately 48.4% cumulative HCQ release over 24 h at pH 7.4. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report of an HCQ-ZnONPs nanocluster system. Biological evaluation demonstrated synergistic in vitro antimalarial activity, indicating enhanced efficacy compared with the parent drug, suggesting that this arises from the integration of HCQ and ZnO nanoclusters while maintaining favorable cytocompatibility in Vero cells. The oxidative stress and anti-inflammatory potential of the hybrid complex was also assessed, highlighting its multifunctional biological profile that may be advantageous for mitigating malaria-associated oxidative stress and inflammatory responses. Molecular docking against PfDHFR-TSfurther supported favorable ligand-target interactions and provided additional insight into the potential molecular basis of the observed biological activity. Conclusions: Collectively, the experimental, theoretical, and mathematical analysis suggests the successful formation of HCQ-ZnONPs with promising anti-inflammatory and antimalarial efficacy, establishing this hybrid nano system as a potential candidate for next-generation antiplasmodial therapy.

articles.titulo: Babesia divergens IgG Antibodies and ABO Blood Types in Humans.
articles.autores: Hirsch IA, Svensson J, … Persson KEM (6 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Babesia is an intraerythrocytic parasite transmitted by ticks or through blood transfusion, and it can cause babesiosis with symptoms such as fever, anemia, and organ failure. The parasite is closely related to the mosquito-borne Plasmodium falciparum, which causes malaria. Several studies have shown that individuals with blood group O have a reduced risk of severe malaria compared to individuals with other ABO blood groups. Whether or not this is also the case for babesiosis has not yet been clearly investigated. In this study, serum samples from over 650 individuals were analyzed using an ELISA assay to detect antibodies against Babesia divergens. The ABO blood groups of the same samples were determined using a conventional method. There was no difference in B. divergens IgG antibody levels between the different ABO blood groups, nor was there any difference in the percentage of positive reactions in the ELISA against B. divergens between the different blood groups. This could indicate that the development and maintenance of B. divergens antibodies are not influenced by ABO blood groups.

articles.titulo: São Tomé and Príncipe on the Verge of Eliminating Lymphatic Filariasis as a Public Health Problem: Evidence from IDA Impact Assessment Surveys.
articles.autores: Bakajika D, Rosário A, … Cano J (13 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Accelerated efforts to eliminate lymphatic filariasis (LF) as a public health problem have been supported by the introduction of the triple-drug regimen of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine and albendazole (IDA) in endemic settings. In São Tomé and Príncipe, nationwide mass drug administration (MDA) with diethylcarbamazine and albendazole was implemented in 2018, followed by IDA in 2019 and 2020. This study assesses progress towards elimination using post-MDA impact assessment surveys conducted after cessation of treatment. Cross-sectional surveys were conducted among adults aged 20 years and older in 2022 and again between December 2024 and January 2025. Circulating filarial antigen (CFA) was detected using the filarial test strip (FTS). Individuals who tested positive were examined for microfilaremia using nocturnal calibrated thick blood smear microscopy. MDA coverage data were obtained from national programme records, and morbidity was assessed by clinical screening during the surveys. Three rounds of nationwide MDA achieved high epidemiological coverage (86.4% in 2018, 74.2% in 2019 and 80.0% in 2020). The impact assessment surveys conducted in 2022 evaluated 14,132 adults, with 21 individuals (0.15%) testing positive for CFA, while the follow-up survey conducted between December 2024 and January 2025 assessed 14,653 adults and detected seven positive cases (0.05%). No microfilariae were detected among the 28 antigen-positive individuals examined using nocturnal calibrated thick blood smears. Clinical screening during the surveys identified 190 cases of lymphoedema and nine cases of hydrocoele. Infection indicators remain well below WHO decision thresholds, suggesting that LF transmission is unlikely to be sustained. São Tomé and Príncipe appears to be close to eliminating LF as a public health problem. However, strengthening morbidity management services will be essential to support the preparation of the national elimination dossier.

articles.titulo: Deep learning convolutional neural networks for morphological identification of field-caught Anopheles stephensi in Ethiopia, using smartphone images of specimens.
articles.autores: Mehta P, Kumar AS, … Acharya S (16 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: Anopheles stephensi, an invasive malaria vector historically confined to South Asia and the Arabian Peninsula, has established reproducing populations across the Horn of Africa and continues to expand its range. Its adaptability to a range of environments, with its impact described most prominently in urban and peri-urban settings, and morphological similarity to native African anophelines, particularly An. gambiae s.l., makes reliable field identification difficult by field entomologists across much of Africa who have had limited prior exposure to the species. Existing molecular methods are impractical for routine field use, creating an urgent need for scalable, accessible identification tools to support surveillance programs responding to this emerging threat.
METHODS: Three deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) classifiers were developed and validated for detecting An. stephensi from photographic images of mosquito specimens collected from sentinel sites across Ethiopia and Uganda, verified for species identity by PCR or morphological identification. VectorCam, a standardized field imaging device, served as the primary imaging platform, with a supplementary handheld smartphone dataset collected using clip-on macro lenses (10X and 15X). An EfficientNet-B1 architecture was fine-tuned using transfer learning from a pretraining dataset of over 60,000 labeled photographs of field-collected mosquito specimens from Uganda. Three classifiers were developed: a VectorCam multiclass classifier distinguishing seven species classes including An. stephensi, a VectorCam binary classifier distinguishing An. stephensi from all other species, and a handheld smartphone binary classifier for photographic images taken using a handheld smartphone. All models were evaluated using 5-fold cross-validation and a majority voting ensemble of the trained classifiers.
RESULTS: Against PCR and morphologically verified ground-truth identifications, the VectorCam multiclass classifier achieved an An. stephensi sensitivity of 98.74% and overall accuracy of 96.02%. The VectorCam binary classifier achieved an An. stephensi sensitivity of 97.48% and a specificity of 99.25%. The handheld binary classifier achieved an An. stephensi sensitivity of 91.09% and a specificity of 84.40%. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping confirmed that classification decisions were driven by wing venation and leg morphology, consistent with established entomological identification criteria.
CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning image classification using VectorCam achieves high accuracy for field detection of An. stephensi, with the binary classifier demonstrating performance suitable for operational vector surveillance, providing a practical, scalable solution for decentralized An. stephensi surveillance across malaria-endemic regions of Africa, reducing reliance on molecular verification or specialist taxonomic training for field-level species identification.

articles.titulo: A reusable neural approach to recombination mapping for model and non-model species.
articles.autores: Korfmann K, Rahnamae N, Mathieson S
articles.resumo_original: Pedigree and crossing experiments can measure crossovers directly and provide the gold standard for recombination mapping, but their cost restricts fine-scale recombination mapping to only a few species. Patterns of linkage disequilibrium (LD) provide an alternative statistical approach for inferring variation in recombination along the genome. LD, however, is confounded by many evolutionary factors, such as demographic changes, life-history traits, and genomic structural variation. We present fastrho , a state-space neural-network estimator trained across a range of simulation-based priors. In simulated bottleneck and expansion scenarios, the fixed checkpoint recovered local map shape without target-specific retraining; comparisons with pyrho used lookup tables constructed under the simulation-generating history. We further evaluated generalizability across multiple species and, to account for additional confounders not represented in the initial training data, designed specialized models for inference in selfing plants, structured Arabis populations, and large- N e malaria-vector populations. A major biological application of the mosquito model was the construction of a five-arm recombination atlas spanning 13 Ag3 populations, providing a detailed view of recombination-rate variation across the dataset. Recombination maps inferred from Ag3 pedigrees provided independent, coarse-scale support for this atlas. Finally, analyses of resistance loci and redpoll bird supergenes demonstrate how selection and structural variation influence LD. Throughout our study, we use experimental maps for independent validation. Together, our results establish fastrho as a flexible framework for robust recombination mapping across diverse biological systems.

articles.titulo: Parasite and host factors associated with malaria parasite liver stage latency.
articles.autores: Kappe S, Zanghi G, … Vaughan A (18 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Plasmodium vivax (Pv) forms dormant liver stage hypnozoites that cause relapsing malaria, a major barrier to Pv eradication. However, parasite-intrinsic mechanisms and host factors governing hypnozoite persistence are mostly unknown. Using purified, cryopreserved Pv Chesson strain sporozoites and Thai field isolates, we established reproducible liver stage infections in human hepatocyte-chimeric mice and primary human hepatocytes, generating persistent and activating hypnozoites. Transcriptomic profiling and RNA-FISH identified the RNA-binding protein PvPUF1 as a conserved hypnozoite-associated marker downregulated upon activation. Liver stage expression of PvPUF1 in P. yoelii (Py) induced quasi-persistent, growth-restricted liver stages in vivo. Comparative in silico analyses identified a PUF1-associated 9-mer RNA motif across Pv and Py liver stage expressed genes, linking PUF1-associated transcripts to the CCR4-NOT deadenylation complex. In addition, spatial transcriptomics revealed that hypnozoites occupy a transcriptionally quiescent host microenvironment distinct from replicating schizonts. Together, these findings identify a molecular regulator underlying hypnozoite persistence, providing a framework for therapeutic strategies targeting hypnozoites.

articles.titulo: Identification of genetic variants in Pfs25 and functional evaluation in mosquito infection.
articles.autores: Orfano A, Cisse A, … Bei AK (32 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Transmission-blocking vaccines (TBVs) are a promising strategy to reduce malaria transmission by targeting parasite stages within the mosquito. However, parasite genetic diversity may limit vaccine efficacy. We used next-generation amplicon deep sequencing to identify non-synonymous single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in Pfs25 from 184 Plasmodium falciparum isolates from Senegal, Tanzania, Ghana, and Burkina Faso. Prioritized SNPs were introduced into P. falciparum via CRISPR-Cas9. For the G116C variant, gametocyte development was evaluated by microscopy and qPCR, and mosquito infectivity was assessed by SMFAs. We identified 26 SNPs, including 24 novel variants. Functional assays showed that the Pfs25 G116C mutation did not affect gametocyte development or exflagellation. SMFA showed no significant differences in oocyst prevalence or intensity between mutant and WT parasites. These findings highlight the importance of integrating genetic surveillance with functional validation to guide the development of effective transmission blocking interventions.

articles.titulo: Harnessing omics to refine taxonomic classification in the malaria vector Anopheles gambiae species complex: a review.
articles.autores: Milugo TK, Kwi P, … Amambua-Ngwa A (5 autores)
articles.resumo_original: The malaria vector Anopheles gambiae s.l. (Diptera: Culicidae) is predominant in sub-Saharan Africa, where it plays a crucial role in transmitting malaria parasites to humans. Hitherto considered a single species, advances in cytogenetics and genomics have unveiled members of the complex as separate species. Whilst these species are morphologically indistinguishable, they are genetically distinct exhibiting significant differences in their ecological interactions and behavior. For example, they display considerable variation in their response to vector control measures and capacity to host malaria parasite, contributing differentially to malaria transmission. Consequently, precise taxonomic identification might help guide control programs against them. However, current approaches used in An. gambiae taxonomic systematics differ in accuracy and sensitivity, making it difficult to correctly delimit species boundaries. In this review, we discuss available taxonomic approaches utilized in An. gambiae complex whilst providing a framework for future taxonomic efforts. We also examine the process of naming a new species within the complex and detail the complexities of existing nomenclature approaches, as well as the prospective challenges they present, while advocating for an alternative approach. We conclude by providing a perspective on the use of a robust integrated approach in classifying and naming species of the An. gambiae complex.

articles.titulo: Insecticide resistance intensity in Anopheles gambiae s.l. populations from Nioro and Ndoffane health districts, Senegal.
articles.autores: Diallo S, Diop M, … Niang EHA (13 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: Malaria remains a major public health concern in sub-Saharan Africa. In Senegal, the increasing resistance of Anopheles gambiae sensu lato (s.l.) to main public health insecticides threatens the effectiveness of long-lasting insecticide-treated nets (LLINs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS). This study aimed to assess insecticide resistance intensity and to determine the distribution of kdr and Ace-1 resistance mutations in wild An. gambiae s.l. populations from Nioro and Ndoffane districts (Kaolack region).
METHODS: Anopheles larvae were collected between September and November 2018 and reared under insectary conditions. Adult females were subjected to World Health Organization (WHO) susceptibility assays using five insecticides: three pyrethroids, one carbamate and one organophosphate. Resistance intensity assays were conducted at 5 × and 10 × diagnostic concentrations. Species within the An. gambiae complex and the East-kdr (1014S), West-kdr (1014F) and Ace-1 (G119S) were identified using Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) technique.
RESULTS: A total of 1830 females An. gambiae s.l. were tested. Widespread resistance to pyrethroids and organophosphates was observed in both districts, while in Ndoffane complete susceptibility to bendiocarb was recorded and in Nioro resistance was observed. Anopheles arabiensis was the predominant species (> 90%), followed by An. gambiae s.s. and An. coluzzii. The frequencies of East-kdr and West-kdr mutations were higher in Ndoffane (40.4% and 30.8%) than in Nioro (10.6% and 13.1%). The Ace-1 (G119S) mutation was detected exclusively in the heterozygous state across all the study populations.
CONCLUSIONS: The studied vectors exhibit multiple insecticide resistance mechanisms, likely driven by combined selection pressures from agricultural and public health insecticide use. Strengthening entomological surveillance and implementing integrated resistance management strategies are essential to preserve the effectiveness of malaria vector control interventions in Senegal.

articles.titulo: Epidemiology of malaria and district-level factors associated with malaria elimination in Sumatra region, Indonesia: a retrospective analysis of surveillance data.
articles.autores: Lestari KD, Surendra H, … Elyazar IRF (15 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: As transmission declines, malaria becomes more spatially and demographically concentrated. This study investigated individual-level malaria characteristics and district-level factors associated with elimination in all 154 districts in Sumatra, Indonesia.
METHODS: We analysed individual-level data of 13,386 reported malaria cases from 2019 to 2021. P. falciparum and P. vivax were confirmed by microscopy or rapid diagnostic test, while probable P. knowlesi was defined as microscopically identified P. knowlesi. Cases were classified as imported if they reported travel to endemic region within 2-4 weeks. Multivariable logistic regression with province as a random effect was used to examine individual-level factors associated with imported cases, and district-level socioeconomic and environmental factors associated with elimination. Spatial clustering of indigenous cases was assessed using Global Moran's I and SaTScan.
RESULTS: Among reported cases, 71.8% (9,617) were P. vivax, 18.4% (2,467) P. falciparum, and 2.8% (369) probable P. knowlesi. Of 11,390 investigated cases, 8,748 (76.8%) were indigenous, 1,741 (15.3%) imported, and 901 (7.9%) unclassified. Imported cases were associated with older age (adjusted odds ratio 1.79, 95%CI 1.42-2.25 for 15-24 years old, and 1.97, 1.59-2.46 for 25-64 years old, compared to < 15 years old), males (1.70, 1.43-2.03), mobile and migrant population-related occupations (1.46, 1.22-1.76), diagnosed at hospitals or clinics (2.32, 1.85-2.91), infected with P. falciparum (1.48, 1.22-1.80), and hospitalised (15.29, 12.66-18.46). At the district level, a higher human development index (1.15, 1.01-1.34), lower historical annual parasite incidence (0.46, 0.29-0.69), and fewer endemic neighbours (0.78, 0.67-0.89) were associated with a higher likelihood of elimination. Spatial analysis revealed clustering tendencies, with localised clusters for P. falciparum, P. vivax, and probable P. knowlesi.
CONCLUSIONS: Dynamics of imported malaria, heterogeneous clusters of local transmission, and lower district-level human development index challenged elimination efforts. This highlights the need for strengthened surveillance and targeted interventions.

articles.titulo: Molecular characterization of antimalarial resistance and hrp2/3 deletions in Plasmodium falciparum strains from Mtwara, Tanzania (2021-2024).
articles.autores: Thapradit P, Pagornrat W, … Imwong M (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: Malaria remains a significant public health challenge in sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia, with Plasmodium falciparum responsible for the majority of infections and deaths, particularly among children aged < 5 years. In Tanzania, the widespread use of antimalarial drugs, such as sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine for preventive therapy and artemisinin-based combination therapies as first-line treatment, has prompted concerns about the emergence and spread of drug resistance. The prolonged use of these drugs may have influenced resistance patterns, varying over time. Moreover, some P. falciparum samples have been reported as rapid diagnostic test (RDT)-negative despite microscopic confirmation of P. falciparum infection, raising questions about whether such false-negative results are due to poor-quality RDT kits or genetic deletions in the parasite.
METHODS: This study investigated drug resistance dynamics and potential false-negative RDT results in P. falciparum by analyzing molecular markers in pfdhps, pfdhfr, pfkelch13, and pfhrp2/3, with the 18S rRNA gene used as a housekeeping control to verify DNA quality and confirm true parasite positivity.
RESULTS: Molecular analysis revealed a decline in the triple pfdhfr mutation paired with double pfdhps mutations, alongside an increase in mixed dhfr-dhps haplotypes (χ2 = 28.94, p < 0.001), indicating ongoing genetic diversification under drug pressure. Wild-type parasites were predominant (56-76%), and most pfkelch13 mutations were located in the non-propeller region, with no validated or candidate mutations associated with artemisinin-resistance detected. P. falciparum-infected samples that were RDT-negative showed a high frequency of both complete and partial deletions in pfhrp2 and pfhrp3, potentially explaining RDT inconsistencies and false-negative results.
CONCLUSIONS: P. falciparum remains the dominant species in this high-transmission region, showing a persistently high rate of antifolate resistance. Significant associations between triple pfdhfr and double pfdhps resistance markers were observed between 2021 and 2024. The continued susceptibility to artemisinin emphasizes the need for ongoing molecular surveillance and monitoring of hrp2/hrp3 deletions to support malaria control strategies in Tanzania.

articles.titulo: Malaria among migrant populations in the Greater Mekong Subregion: a scoping review of evidence and implications for malaria elimination.
articles.autores: Aung PL, Zay Ya K, … Sattabongkot J (8 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: Countries in the Greater Mekong Subregion (GMS) have made substantial progress toward malaria elimination, with a regional goal of achieving elimination by 2030. However, residual transmission persists, particularly among migrant and mobile populations in border and forested areas, who often experience increased exposure and limited access to healthcare and preventive interventions. This scoping review aimed to synthesize evidence on malaria epidemiology, healthcare access, prevention practices, and health system challenges among migrant and mobile populations in the GMS.
METHODS: A scoping review was conducted following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. Two electronic databases (PubMed and Scopus) were searched from inception to March 2026. Studies reporting on malaria among migrant or mobile populations in GMS countries were included. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Findings were synthesized narratively and organized into six thematic domains.
RESULTS: A total of 847 records were identified, of which 52 studies met the inclusion criteria. Malaria burden among migrant and mobile populations was generally low but highly heterogeneous, with persistent transmission concentrated in border and forested areas and evidence of asymptomatic and submicroscopic infections indicating hidden reservoirs of transmission. Across the included studies, migrant and mobile populations experienced intersecting structural vulnerabilities, including cross-border mobility, precarious employment, legal and administrative barriers, language barriers, and limited access to health services, that contributed to delayed diagnosis and treatment, inconsistent uptake of preventive measures, and reliance on informal or cross-border healthcare. Preventive practices often remained suboptimal because of occupational and mobility-related constraints. Existing interventions, including community-based services and mobile health approaches, showed promise but remained limited in coverage and evaluation, underscoring persistent challenges for surveillance, service delivery, and cross-border coordination.
CONCLUSIONS: Migrant and mobile populations remain a critical challenge to malaria elimination in the GMS. Residual transmission is sustained by asymptomatic infections, structural barriers to healthcare access, suboptimal preventive practices, and high mobility. Achieving malaria elimination by 2030 will require tailored and equitable strategies that strengthen surveillance, expand flexible and accessible service delivery, and enhance cross-border collaboration for migrant and mobile populations.

articles.titulo: Autochthonous Plasmodium falciparum malaria in a high-altitude, non-endemic region of Ethiopia: a case report.
articles.autores: Derse TK, Asgai AS, … Lidetu T (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: Malaria transmission in Ethiopia is traditionally limited to altitudes below 2000 m. Debark Town, situated at 2850 m, is a high-altitude highland fringe area characterized by a cold climate and has historically been considered a non-endemic zone. This report describes a rare, locally acquired case of Plasmodium falciparum in this extreme environment.
CASE PRESENTATION: A 15-year-old Ethiopian female of Amhara ethnicity resident in Debark Town presented with a 5-day history of high-grade fever (39.5 °C), headache, and vomiting. Significantly, she reported no history of travel to known malaria-endemic regions. Clinical examination revealed tachycardia (140 bpm) and hypotension (90/50 mmHg). Laboratory investigations showed profound thrombocytopenia (20 × 109/L). P. falciparum infection was confirmed via a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and thick blood smear (0.14% parasitemia). Despite the hypotension and low platelet count, the patient remained alert and was classified as having high risk but uncomplicated malaria.
MANAGEMENT AND OUTCOME: The patient was treated with a weight-based, six-dose regimen of Artemether-Lumefantrine (ACT) and supportive fluid resuscitation. Rapid clinical response was observed; apyrexia was achieved within 24 h. A follow-up assessment at 1 week confirmed full clinical and hematological recovery with negative parasitology.
CONCLUSIONS: This case highlights the shifting epidemiology of malaria in the Ethiopian highlands, where traditional "altitude barriers" may no longer provide absolute protection. Clinicians in high-altitude zones must maintain a high index of clinical suspicion for malaria in febrile patients, regardless of travel history, to ensure early diagnosis and prevent severe outcomes in non-immune populations.

articles.titulo: Low-frequency parasitized cells in bone marrow alter myelopoiesis following immunization with the live attenuated Leishmania major Cen -/- vaccine.
articles.autores: Azodi N, Pacheco-Fernandez T, … Gannavaram S (14 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Leishmaniasis lacks an effective vaccine. We developed a live-attenuated Leishmania major Centrin-deficient strain (LmCen -/-) that is safe and protective in murine and canine models through IFN-γ-producing effector T cells. Because persistent low-level infection supports durable immunity, we investigated latent parasites and immune remodeling in the bone marrow. Dual single-cell RNA sequencing detected parasitized bone marrow cells 28 days after intradermal inoculation with either virulent LmWT or attenuated LmCen -/-. Flow cytometry showed increased myelopoiesis following LmCen -/- immunization compared with LmWT infection. Cell-cell communication analysis implicated enhanced granulin-Sort3 signaling as a potential driver of this response. Bone marrow monocytes from LmCen -/--immunized mice efficiently cleared virulent LmWT parasites in co-culture, consistent with the induction of trained innate immunity. These findings identify the bone marrow as an active site of anti-Leishmania immune programming and suggest that LmCen -/- vaccination promotes durable protection through coordinated adaptive and innate mechanisms.

articles.titulo: A voltage-gated porin PPE1 regulates secretion and drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
articles.revista: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
articles.autores: Yadav M, C A NF, … Gokhale RS (13 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) remains a formidable clinical hurdle, compounded by the fact that the pathways by which antibiotics penetrate its multilayered cell envelope remain incompletely mapped. We identify PPE1 as a voltage-gated outer-membrane porin that mediates the secretion of kupyaphores while also facilitating the uptake of the frontline anti-tubercular drug isoniazid (INH). Genome-wide association analysis of 38,038 clinical isolates links ppe1 mutations with INH resistance, highlighting its clinical relevance. Consistent with this, the Mtb Δppe1 mutant shows increased tolerance to INH, accompanied by markedly reduced intracellular accumulation of INH compared with the wild-type strain. The Δppe1 strain exhibits attenuated infection, impaired growth, and reduced virulence in a murine infection model. Electron microscopy, molecular modeling, and single-channel electrophysiology reveal that PPE1 assembles into an unusual pentameric α-helical channel, distinct from classical β-barrel bacterial porins. Together, our findings identify PPE1 as a key determinant of mycobacterial membrane permeability that coordinates metallophore secretion and also antibiotic influx. This work uncovers a previously unrecognized mechanism governing Mtb physiology, virulence, and drug susceptibility, providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

articles.titulo: Powerhouses of lethality: mitochondria in macrophage antimicrobial activity.
articles.autores: McFadden MJ, O'Meara TR, O'Riordan MX
articles.resumo_original: Macrophages employ multiple strategies to dispatch phagocytosed microbes, including bombardment with toxic compounds and radicals, or the deprivation of key nutrients. The lethality of macrophages depends on their ability to regulate levels of microbicidal effectors and proper targeting of these effectors to the phagosome, where many intracellular pathogens are detained. Mitochondria play important roles in establishing an antimicrobial phagosomal environment in macrophages, playing roles in both the production and targeting of these effectors. In response to infection, the mitochondrial network undergoes dramatic structural and functional perturbations that modulate macrophage microbicidal potential. As central coordinators of cellular metabolism, mitochondria control the abundance of metabolites that can either be toxic to ingested microbes or necessary for their growth. Mitochondria are also prolific producers of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which play direct roles in killing microbes and serve as signaling molecules to coordinate antimicrobial responses. While mitochondria are also known to play extensive roles in regulating cytokine production and proinflammatory responses, this review will focus on highlighting mechanisms by which mitochondria manipulate the macrophage microbicidal milieu.

articles.titulo: Platelet-macrophage crosstalk in cardiac inflammation and remodeling.
articles.revista: Biochim Biophys Acta Mol Cell Res
articles.autores: Ahmad F, Qaisar R, … Ansari AW (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Cardiac injury and chronic heart disease are increasingly recognized as multicellular processes driven by dynamic interactions between immune and thrombotic signaling networks. Although platelets and macrophages have been extensively studied individually, the molecular mechanisms through which their reciprocal interactions regulate cardiac inflammation and remodeling remain incompletely defined. A comprehensive understanding of this cellular crosstalk is needed to define the signaling pathways that couple acute injury responses to chronic maladaptive remodeling. Among these interactions, platelet-macrophage crosstalk has emerged as an important regulator of inflammatory responses and tissue remodeling within the injured myocardium. Beyond their traditional roles in hemostasis and innate immunity, platelets communicate with macrophages through adhesion molecules, soluble mediators, and extracellular vesicles, thereby modulating macrophage activation and functional reprogramming. Platelet-derived mediators, including P-selectin, CD40L, PF4 (CXCL4), CCL5, and platelet-derived extracellular vesicles, modulate macrophage inflammatory signaling, cytokine production, redox balance, metabolic reprogramming, and pro-fibrotic responses relevant to cardiac remodeling. During acute myocardial injury, these interactions facilitate immune-cell recruitment, efferocytosis, and tissue repair, whereas persistent platelet-macrophage communication promotes chronic inflammation, extracellular matrix remodeling, and progression to heart failure. This review summarizes current molecular insights into platelet-macrophage interactions, focusing on receptor-mediated signaling, extracellular vesicle cargo transfer, immunometabolic regulation, and redox-dependent pathways. We also discuss emerging evidence linking this axis to trained immunity and inflammatory memory and highlight potential molecular targets for modulating maladaptive immune remodeling in cardiovascular disease.

articles.titulo: [LGALS3 is an efferocytosis-related biomarker and potential traditional Chinese medicine therapeutic target for diabetic kidney disease complicated with heart failure].
articles.revista: Nan Fang Yi Ke Da Xue Xue Bao
articles.autores: Hu D, Guo H, … Nie X (7 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
OBJECTIVES: To explore the immune efferocytosis mechanisms of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) complicated with chronic heart failure (CHF) in light of the glucose heart kidney axis and predict the "same treatment for different diseases" strategy using traditional Chinese medicine (TCM).
METHODS: DKD and CHF transcriptome data from public databases were integrated to construct a core gene set using differential expression and weighted gene co-expression network analysis (WGCNA). The hub genes were intersected with an efferocytosis-related gene set, validated with external datasets, and functionally enriched. The Coremine Medical database and molecular docking were used to predict the regulatory TCMs, their properties, and affinities between the active ingredients and their targets. Clinical serum samples were collected form patients with DKD, CHF, and DKD+CHF and healthy individuals for detecting galectin 3 (LGALS3) levels.
RESULTS: Fifty comorbidity core genes were identified, which were enriched mainly in the PI3K Akt, TNF, AGE RAGE, and oxidative phosphorylation pathways. LGALS3 was identified as a key efferocytosis-associated hub gene with differential expression in the validation set. The prediction results included 216 TCMs predominantly exhibiting cold or warm properties with bitter, sweet or pungent flavors and liver, lung, spleen and kidney meridian tropisms. Molecular docking suggested strong binding between the key ingredients (e.g., quercetin) and LGALS3. Serum LGALS3 levels were significantly higher in patients with DKD+CHF than in those with DKD or CHF alone or healthy controls (all P<0.001). After adjusting for covariates, comorbid status remained independently and positively associated with LGALS3 (β=51.20, P<0.001), exceeding the independent contribution of NT proBNP.
CONCLUSIONS: DKD-CHF is associated with inflammatory/metabolic abnormalities and impairment of efferocytosis-mediated immune clearance. LGALS3 is a critical node connecting inflammatory pathways to target organ efferocytosis dysfunction. The predicted TCMs highlight the TCM therapeutic principles of "supplementing Qi, clearing the heat and resolving stasis" and may regulate efferocytosis and the immunometabolic microenvironment by targeting LGALS3.

articles.titulo: Beyond Targeted Delivery: The Emerging Immunomodulatory Landscape of Antibody-Oligonucleotide Conjugates.
articles.autores: Wang Y, Wang S, Wang H
articles.resumo_original: Antibody-oligonucleotide conjugates (AOCs) are usually viewed as delivery vehicles that carry nucleic-acid payloads to defined cell populations for gene silencing or gene regulation. Existing reviews concentrate on delivery systems, tumour-directed therapy and extrahepatic oligonucleotide delivery, while the intrinsic immunomodulatory activity of AOCs has received far less attention. Conjugation couples antibody-mediated targeting with the innate immune-stimulating activity of the payload, a property that most current AOCs seldom exploit. This review repositions AOCs as active immune regulators. Three emerging immunoregulatory applications are examined in detail: vaccine-adjuvant construction, neutrophil-driven innate immune activation, and immunometabolic reprogramming. Structure-activity relationships linking AOC design to immune potency are summarized, and their immune mechanisms are distinguished from those of free oligonucleotides and unconjugated antibodies. Based on preclinical and in vitro evidence, AOCs act as multifunctional immunomodulators rather than passive cargo carriers. Two sources of immune activity are distinguished: direct immunostimulation by the conjugated payload, and effects secondary to targeted delivery. These findings still await clinical confirmation. Key barriers to translation, including conjugation efficiency, mechanistic gaps and manufacturing bottlenecks, are discussed. Prospective applications include engineered vaccines, anti-infective innate therapy, tumour microenvironment remodelling and autoimmune intervention, pending further validation. This review provides a conceptual framework for developing next-generation AOC-based immune adjuvants and precision immunotherapeutics.

articles.titulo: Microbiota-Associated Metabolites as Immunometabolic Regulators of Glomerular Inflammation: Disease-Specific Mechanisms and Therapeutic Opportunities.
articles.autores: Hou F, Yang L, … Liu B (7 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: Immunoglobulin A nephropathy (IgAN), membranous nephropathy (MN), and lupus nephritis (LN) are immune-mediated glomerular diseases in which dysregulated adaptive immunity converges with innate inflammatory and filtration-barrier injury. Clinical relapse and incomplete recovery despite upstream immune control motivate investigation of additional injury modifiers.
MAIN BODY: This review evaluates five microbiota-associated metabolite families-short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), tryptophan-derived metabolites, aromatic amino acid-derived uremic solutes, trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO), and bile acids-across three modules: immune-tolerance failure, innate inflammatory amplification, and filtration-barrier disruption. In IgAN, multi-omics data showing preserved or elevated systemic acetate with reduced glomerular free fatty acid receptor 2/3 (FFAR2/FFAR3)-associated signaling suggest impaired renal SCFA sensing, but do not establish receptor competence as the dominant target. In MN, disease-specific studies support podocyte injury mediated by complement C3a and its receptor (C3a/C3aR) and complement-associated NOD-, LRR- and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3)-caspase-1-gasdermin D (GSDMD) pyroptosis as related injury processes, whereas proposed SCFA-regulatory T cell (Treg)-B-cell and SCFA-inflammasome interactions remain largely hypothesis-generating; experimental Lactobacillus-indole-aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) data provide preliminary evidence. In LN, microbiota-dependent tryptophan pathway perturbation and treatment-associated metabolomic changes support the kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio as a readily measurable candidate biomarker requiring prospective validation. Across diseases, interpretation requires separating microbial production from renal retention, metabolite abundance from receptor signaling competence, and total from unbound exposure for protein-bound solutes.
CONCLUSION: Microbiota-associated metabolites constitute a plausible immunometabolic layer rather than established causal pathways in immune-mediated glomerular disease. Priorities include disease-specific longitudinal phenotyping, compartment-resolved metabolite measurement, target-engagement studies, and biomarker-embedded clinical trials before therapeutic claims are advanced.

articles.titulo: Beyond Neuroinflammation: Targeting the Microbe-Barrier-Brain Axis Through Precision Nutrition in Neurological Long COVID (Neuro-PASC).
articles.autores: Velázquez De Castro-Bono A, Castro-Luna G, Guil-Guerrero JL
articles.resumo_original: Post-acute Neurological Sequelae of SARS-CoV-2 infection (Neuro-PASC) contribute substantially to Long COVID-related disability, with cognitive impairment, chronic fatigue, dysautonomia, and neuropsychiatric symptoms among its most debilitating manifestations. Although its pathogenesis remains incompletely understood, evidence implicates persistent immune activation, intestinal barrier dysfunction, microbiota dysbiosis, microbiome-derived metabolic alterations, mitochondrial dysfunction, and neuroimmune interactions in sustaining neuroinflammation and neurological impairment. This narrative review examines precision nutrition as a potential pathway-oriented strategy for Neuro-PASC. We synthesise evidence linking the gut microbiota, intestinal permeability, immunometabolic pathways, mitochondrial function, and neurological outcomes, while evaluating nutritional interventions targeting these mechanisms. We focus on candidate biomarkers, including serum zonulin, fatty acid-binding protein 2 (FABP2), faecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), and the kynurenine-to-tryptophan ratio, which may support patient stratification and personalised nutritional strategies. We also propose a stepwise framework involving dietary stabilisation, functional foods, targeted supplementation, and microbiome-based interventions, alongside practical considerations for post-exertional symptom exacerbation, dysautonomia, and mast cell-related symptoms. Finally, we identify priorities for future research, including multi-omics integration, artificial intelligence, digital health, and biomarker-stratified randomised controlled trials. Because current evidence remains predominantly observational and mechanistic, precision nutrition should be considered a complementary strategy requiring rigorous clinical validation.

articles.titulo: c-Myc Links TGF-β Signaling to Metabolic Control of HIV Reactivation in OM10.1 Cells.
articles.autores: Harrison-Gleason J, Kim J, Martinelli E
articles.resumo_original: Antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses HIV replication but does not eliminate persistent viral reservoirs, which can rapidly reseed viremia following treatment interruption. We previously showed that blockade of transforming growth factor beta (TGF-β) signaling in vivo promotes SIV latency reversal and is associated with reversal of cellular metabolic quiescence. Here, using the provirally infected promyelocytic OM10.1 cell line, we investigated the cell-intrinsic mechanisms through which TGF-β regulates HIV reactivation. TGF-β inhibited proviral reactivation following stimulation with distinct latency-reversing agents, and this effect was reversed by pharmacologic inhibition of TGF-β signaling. TGF-β reduced HIV transcription without suppressing TNF-α-induced NF-κB activation, suggesting inhibition through an alternative mechanism. Bulk RNA sequencing revealed broad suppression of c-Myc-associated pathways, oxidative phosphorylation, and mTORC1 signaling. Functional metabolic profiling confirmed marked reductions in both glycolytic and mitochondrial ATP production and decreased mitochondrial membrane polarization. Consistent with a functional link between metabolism and viral reactivation, mitochondrial uncoupling strongly inhibited HIV expression. Finally, MYC overexpression completely rescued HIV transcription and partially restored p24 production in TGF-β-treated cells. Together, these findings identify a cell-intrinsic mechanism through which TGF-β restrains HIV reactivation by imposing a metabolically quiescent state, mediated at least in part through suppression of c-Myc.

articles.titulo: Lactate-Driven Biphasic Reprogramming of Macrophage Immune Responses.
articles.autores: Guo Q, Ren P, … Fang C (10 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Lactate is a metabolic substrate, an extracellular signaling molecule, and a precursor for protein lactylation, with diverse effects on macrophage immunity. Evidence from infection, tissue injury, efferocytosis, and cancer indicates that lactate-associated pathways can amplify inflammation, support resolution and tissue repair, or sustain immune suppression. These outcomes depend on the timing, cellular source and compartment, chemical formulation and pH, transport and receptor engagement, and the chemistry and targets of lactylation. In this narrative review, we critically synthesize the biochemical foundations of lactate metabolism and lactyl-group donation and examine the mechanisms underlying these distinct macrophage responses. We distinguish model-specific biphasic responses from a universal sequence of early inflammation followed by resolution, and separate reparative programs from impaired antimicrobial or antitumor immunity. We also evaluate evidence for histone and non-histone lactylation, emphasizing the limits of metabolic perturbations and chromatin associations for establishing site-specific causality. This framework identifies experimental variables that should be controlled and supports context-selective investigation of lactate-related therapeutic targets in inflammatory diseases and cancer.

articles.titulo: Dietary Vitamin Intake and Cognitive Performance in Adults with Long COVID: The BioICOPER Study.
articles.autores: Arjol D, Arroyo-Romero S, … BioICOPER Investigators Group (11 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Background: Long COVID (LC) is associated with persistent cognitive symptoms, frequently described as brain fog, and with inflammatory, immunometabolic, and energetic mechanisms potentially involved in cognitive functioning. Vitamins participate in biological processes relevant to brain function, but the relationship between habitual dietary vitamin intake and cognitive performance in LC remains poorly studied. Objective: To analyze the relationship between dietary vitamin intake and cognitive performance in adults with LC, considering both objective performance and self-reported cognition. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted in 304 adults with LC. Vitamin intake from foods and beverages was estimated using the EVIDENT seven-day dietary record, previously compared with a validated food-frequency questionnaire. Objective cognitive performance was assessed using normative scores from the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and the Memory Index Score (MIS), as well as MoCA domains and items. Self-reported cognition was assessed using the 30-item Memory Failures of Everyday Questionnaire (MFE-30) and the cognitive subscale of the Modified Fatigue Impact Scale (MFIS). Primary global associations were examined using multiple linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors, whereas bounded MoCA domains were analyzed using proportional-odds ordinal regression and binary item-level outcomes using logistic regression. Benjamini-Hochberg correction was applied within prespecified families of contrasts. Results: No associations between vitamin intake and global normative cognitive performance remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Median MoCA and MIS scores were 24.00 (IQR, 21.00-26.00) and 11.00 (IQR, 9.00-13.00), respectively. Normative MoCA and MIS scores showed medians of -0.32 (IQR, -0.82 to 0.19) and -0.32 (IQR, -0.76 to 0.14), respectively. Most participants (95.1%) met the dietary reference value for vitamin B3. In secondary ordinal analyses, higher vitamin B3 intake was associated with better MoCA language performance in the fully adjusted model (OR per 1 SD = 2.18, 95% CI 1.45-3.27, p < 0.001, q = 0.0116). No associations remained significant after FDR correction for everyday cognitive complaints, cognitive fatigue, or MoCA Memory and MoCA Multiple scores. Conclusions: In adults with LC, the primary analyses did not identify FDR-significant associations between habitual dietary vitamin intake and global normative cognitive performance. The secondary vitamin B3-language association requires independent confirmation and does not establish a cognitive benefit of higher intake or supplementation. These findings require confirmation in longitudinal studies incorporating nutritional biomarkers, information on supplementation, and broader neuropsychological assessment.

articles.titulo: The Aldosterone-Immune Axis in Primary Aldosteronism: Linking Adrenal Pathogenesis to Systemic Inflammation and Target-Organ Damage.
articles.autores: Zaidi NE, Azizan EA, Ali A
articles.resumo_original: Primary aldosteronism (PA) is the most common endocrine cause of secondary hypertension and is increasingly recognised as a systemic disorder extending beyond haemodynamic dysregulation. Accumulating evidence suggests that chronic autonomous aldosterone excess promotes maladaptive immune activation, establishing an aldosterone-immune axis that may contribute to cardiovascular, renal, and metabolic injury independently of blood pressure elevation. In some patients, glucocorticoid co-secretion may further amplify tissue-specific mineralocorticoid receptor (MR) signalling. Human and experimental studies indicate that aldosterone modulates both innate and adaptive immunity. Patients with PA demonstrate altered monocyte transcriptional profiles, enhanced vascular inflammatory activity, and increased pro-inflammatory cytokine signalling in monocyte-derived macrophages compared with blood-pressure-matched essential hypertension controls. Experimental models further show that sustained aldosterone exposure promotes macrophage M1 polarisation, dendritic cell activation, Th17 expansion, and regulatory T-cell suppression. These inflammatory changes are accompanied by oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, fibroblast activation, and extracellular matrix remodelling across cardiovascular and renal tissues. Emerging evidence is also consistent with a role for trained innate immunity, whereby prolonged aldosterone exposure may induce persistent epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming of monocytes and macrophages. Whether such reprogramming persists after biochemical correction by adrenalectomy or MR antagonism in human PA has not yet been directly demonstrated and remains an important open question. If confirmed, these mechanisms may help explain the partial irreversibility of target-organ damage despite successful treatment. This review synthesises current evidence linking adrenal somatic pathogenesis to systemic immune dysregulation and target-organ injury in PA. We propose that PA should be viewed not solely as a hypertensive disorder, but as a chronic fibro-inflammatory endocrine disease with important implications for early diagnosis, risk stratification, and targeted therapy. Future prospective human studies are needed to confirm the mechanistic hierarchy proposed and to identify the immunological targets most amenable to therapeutic intervention.

articles.titulo: Advancing Tuberculosis Vaccination: Immunological Insights and Emerging Strategies for Improved Protection.
articles.autores: Zhang Z, Sanchez C, … Chacon J (8 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Tuberculosis (TB) remains one of the leading causes of infectious disease mortality worldwide despite widespread Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination and decades of control efforts. The limited and variable efficacy of current vaccination strategies, particularly against adult pulmonary disease, highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the host immune mechanisms that determine protection against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. While traditional approaches to TB vaccine development have largely focused on pathogen-specific immunity and clinical efficacy, emerging evidence suggests that successful TB control may depend equally on the strategic modulation of host immune responses. This narrative review examines the immunological basis of TB vaccination, emphasizing how contemporary vaccine platforms reshape both innate and adaptive immunity. We discuss the roles of trained immunity, T-cell function, immune memory, and mucosal immune responses in mediating protection, as well as the mechanisms by which M. tuberculosis evades immune surveillance. The review further explores next-generation vaccine technologies, including protein-adjuvant, viral-vectored, live-attenuated, and mRNA-based vaccines, highlighting their distinct immunological targets. Particular attention is given to mucosal immunity, systems vaccinology, and the ongoing search for reliable correlates of protection, which collectively offer new opportunities to improve vaccine design and evaluation. Finally, we examine host-directed immunomodulatory approaches, immune-engineering strategies, and precision vaccinology as emerging paradigms for TB prevention. By reframing TB vaccines as instruments for immune reprogramming rather than solely pathogen-specific interventions, this review provides an integrated perspective on how advances in immunology may accelerate progress toward global TB control and the goals of the WHO End TB Strategy.

articles.titulo: Glucocorticoid Receptor Alpha as an Integrative Regulator of Host Defense: A Systems-Level Review and Framework for Immune Regulation and Homeostatic Correction.
articles.autores: Meduri GU
articles.resumo_original: Current concepts recognize that effective host defense depends on coordinated interactions among innate and adaptive immunity, inflammatory signaling, immunometabolic regulation, and multiple complementary adaptive biological processes. However, far less attention has focused on the regulatory systems that integrate these diverse responses across the evolving phases of the host response. This Review proposes that glucocorticoid receptor alpha (GRα) functions as a systems-level integrative regulator that may contribute to the integration of immune signaling, antimicrobial competence, mitochondrial bioenergetics, inflammatory regulation, and other adaptive processes across partially overlapping adaptive phases of homeostatic correction. A central premise is that these phase-specific actions are shaped by dynamic changes in chromatin accessibility and transcription-factor interactions, providing a molecular basis for differential GRα regulation throughout the adaptive response. Rather than functioning solely as a transcriptional regulator of inflammation, GRα influences biological processes involved in pathogen sensing, NF-κB/AP-1 signaling, immunometabolic adaptation, innate and adaptive immune responses, endothelial and epithelial barrier integrity, lymphatic function, tissue repair, and the transition from early host defense to inflammatory resolution and restoration of physiological homeostasis. These integrated biological processes are organized within the proposed Priming, Modulatory, and Restorative phases of homeostatic correction. By synthesizing evidence across multiple physiological systems, this Review provides a biologically plausible model for understanding how GRα-associated regulatory mechanisms may contribute to immune effectiveness, disease tolerance, host-defense outcomes, and adaptive recovery during infection and critical illness. The proposed model generates testable hypotheses to guide future mechanistic investigation and the development of precision therapeutic strategies.

articles.titulo: From emergency myelopoiesis to trained immunity? Reframing post-stroke myeloid reprogramming along the brain-bone marrow axis.
articles.autores: Wei T, Wang Y
articles.resumo_original: Ischemic stroke rapidly mobilizes myeloid cells from anatomically distinct bone-marrow niches, while emerging evidence indicates that severe cerebral injury can also leave a durable imprint on hematopoiesis. These observations have encouraged the use of the term trained immunity in stroke biology, but acute myeloid expansion is not equivalent to innate immune memory. In this Mini review, we distinguish acute myeloid activation, myelopoietic responses consistent with emergency myelopoiesis, and central trained immunity involving hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs). We use an operational four-feature framework-persistence, progenitor involvement, epigenetic or metabolic reprogramming, and functional recall-to grade the strength of current evidence. We consider a sequential transition from emergency myelopoiesis to trained immunity as one testable possibility rather than an established pathway, while allowing for parallel or independent mechanisms. The key unresolved questions are where durable memory is stored, when acute hematopoietic adaptation becomes stabilized, and which outputs are maladaptive versus reparative. Resolving these boundaries is essential before marrow-directed immunomodulation can be translated to patients with ischemic stroke.

articles.titulo: Obesity-driven inflammation and immune dysregulation in cancer development and progression.
articles.autores: Pandey P, Struder JF, … Altwegg KA (7 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Obesity increases the risk and progression of at least 13 types of cancer. Although the epidemiologic links between excess adiposity and these cancers are well documented, the biological mechanisms linking obesity to carcinogenesis and tumor progression remain incompletely understood. White adipose tissue in obesity is a source of inflammatory and immunosuppressive signals that act systemically, driving metabolic, inflammatory, and immune dysfunction whose consequences differ across tumor types. As adipose tissue expands and adipocytes enlarge, the blood supply becomes inadequate, leading to hypoxia, fibrosis, lipolytic stress, macrophage recruitment, and chronic low-grade inflammation. These obesity-induced perturbations generate endocrine, cytokine, lipid, and metabolic signals that act systemically, within the tumor microenvironment (TME), and/or cell-intrinsically to activate oncogenic and tumor-promoting pathways. The same signals reshape innate and adaptive immunity, promoting tumor-permissive macrophage states and myeloid-derived suppressor cell expansion, while the effector arms weaken as antigen presentation, natural killer cell and T cell function all decline. This review synthesizes current evidence linking obesity-associated inflammation and immune dysregulation to cancer initiation, progression, and treatment responses across multiple obesity-related cancers. Emphasis is placed on adipose tissue inflammation, myeloid cell biology, T cell immunometabolism, endocrine-inflammatory crosstalk, and the relationship between obesity and immunotherapy. Finally, we discuss translational opportunities for preventing or intercepting obesity-related cancers, including weight loss achieved through lifestyle, surgical, or pharmacologic approaches, with an emphasis on GLP-1 receptor agonists given their substantial efficacy, rapid clinical uptake, and potential to reshape obesity-related cancer prevention and survivorship strategies. Defining the metabolic, immune, and inflammatory phenotypes that drive obesity-associated cancer risk and progression will be essential for developing more precise, mechanism-based strategies for prevention, treatment, and survivorship care.

articles.titulo: Metabolic stress and macrophage efferocytosis in osteoarthritis: mechanisms and therapeutic implications.
articles.autores: Wu H, Yuan D, … Liu S (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Metabolic disturbances contribute to osteoarthritis through mechanisms that extend beyond increased mechanical loading, yet their effects on inflammatory resolution remain incompletely understood. Macrophage efferocytosis-the recognition, engulfment, and degradation of apoptotic cells-provides a potential link between metabolic stress and persistent synovitis. This Mini Review examines how obesity and hyperglycemia disrupt synovial macrophage clearance and evaluates the rationale for therapeutic restoration. Human observations and experimental osteoarthritis studies implicate reduced growth arrest-specific 6 signaling and hyperglycemia-associated CD11b lactylation in defective apoptotic-cell recognition and uptake. Complementary evidence from other inflammatory conditions identifies membrane trafficking, mitochondrial adaptation, and lysosomal cargo processing as additional determinants of clearance competence. Importantly, glycolysis and lactate have context-dependent effects: although lactylation can impair recognition, adaptive lactate signaling supports repeated engulfment and expansion of pro-resolving macrophages. This distinction challenges indiscriminate glycolytic inhibition and favors interventions matched to the affected clearance step. Defective efferocytosis may amplify synovitis through persistence of cellular debris and loss of resolution-promoting signals, thereby creating an environment unfavorable to cartilage homeostasis. Emerging receptor-directed, metabolic, and intra-articular delivery strategies offer opportunities to restore clearance, but clinical validation remains necessary. Translation will require identification of susceptible macrophage populations, functional assessment of the complete efferocytic process, and demonstration that clearance recovery mediates meaningful improvements in joint structure and symptoms.

articles.titulo: Lactate dynamics at the Pseudomonas aeruginosa-host interface: bacterial metabolism, host defense, and emerging links to histone lactylation.
articles.autores: Jian Y, Wu Z, … Wang K (7 autores)
articles.resumo_original: At the Pseudomonas aeruginosa-host interface, lactate is both a host immunometabolic product and a preferred bacterial carbon source. Its local concentration reflects host production, bacterial utilization, transport, and clearance rather than inflammation alone. P. aeruginosa uses D- and L-lactate through stereospecific, conditionally regulated systems. It preferentially consumes lactate in human burn-wound exudate, and this capacity contributes to early intracellular survival in macrophages. Lactate-associated acidity also increases bacterial vesicle release and quinolone signaling, weakening antimicrobial-peptide activity independently of chromatin modification. On the host side, bacterial L-lactate utilization and virulence-factor-associated suppression of epithelial glycolysis lower epithelial lactate and histone H3 lysine 18 lactylation (H3K18la). These changes are linked to disrupted RNA regulation and impaired ciliary clearance. In macrophages, the quorum-sensing signal 2-aminoacetophenone (2-AA) reprograms bioenergetics, autophagy, and lipid metabolism, promoting tolerance and intracellular persistence. A separate hypothesis connecting 2-AA to increased macrophage lactate and H3K18la is supported only by a supplement abstract and requires full-length validation. Histone lactylation is therefore an emerging extension of this biology. This narrative review follows two linked strands: bacterial lactate utilization and lactate-associated changes in host defense. It distinguishes established metabolic effects from proposed lactylation-dependent mechanisms and considers potential therapeutic directions and their trade-offs. These include targeting bacterial lactate utilization, airway acidity, host transport or modification enzymes, and 2-AA-associated tolerance. Any benefit must be assessed against the possibility of supplying bacterial nutrients or worsening host injury.

articles.titulo: Cachexia and Sarcopenia in Patients with Coexisting Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease and Pulmonary Tuberculosis.
articles.autores: Oskin D, Kotlyarov S
articles.resumo_original: Malnutrition, loss of muscle mass, and reduced muscle strength are common but underrecognized conditions in tuberculosis (TB) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). These abnormalities may persist after completion of TB treatment, and a normal or elevated body mass index does not exclude muscle depletion. Unlike the extensively studied conditions of hyperglycemia and obesity, the catabolic end of the spectrum of metabolic disturbances in coexisting TB and COPD remains insufficiently investigated. This narrative review focuses on cachexia and sarcopenia in patients with coexisting TB and COPD (TB-COPD). It examines the roles of systemic inflammation, immunometabolic remodeling, mitochondrial dysfunction, disturbances in protein metabolism and endocrine regulation, and ceramide signaling. Because direct evidence in TB-COPD is scarce, findings from TB or post-tuberculosis lung disease without confirmed COPD and from COPD alone are used as indirect evidence, and the level of evidence is indicated for each mechanism. The diagnostic approach is organized around current clinical guidelines and includes assessment of nutritional status, diagnosis of malnutrition using the Global Leadership Initiative on Malnutrition (GLIM) criteria, identification of sarcopenia using European Working Group on Sarcopenia in Older People 2 (EWGSOP2) or Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS) criteria, pulmonary function testing to distinguish post-tuberculosis airflow obstruction from COPD, and evaluation for reversible causes of muscle weakness. The main treatment approaches are correction of malnutrition, pulmonary rehabilitation, and treatment of the underlying respiratory disease. The effectiveness of interventions is assessed through changes in muscle strength, physical performance, body weight, and body composition. The evidence base for patients with coexisting TB and COPD remains limited; most studies have investigated each disease separately. The efficacy of pharmacological agents targeting the molecular mechanisms of muscle wasting has not been established in this population. Priorities for future research include prospective assessment of muscle function in TB-COPD cohorts and the development of personalized strategies for nutritional and rehabilitation support.

articles.titulo: Beyond Histocompatibility: Donor Tissue Immune States and Their Role in Heart Transplantation.
articles.autores: Urbanowicz T, Kowalewski M, … Raffa GM (4 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Heart transplantation transfers not only donor alloantigens and functional myocardium but also a pre-existing tissue environment shaped by resident immune, vascular, stromal, and parenchymal populations. This review examines the hypothesis that the biological state of donor tissue influences subsequent recipient immunity and contributes to heterogeneity in allograft outcomes. Donor-resident macrophages, endothelial cells, fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, and tissue-resident lymphocytes constitute an immunologically active myocardial niche that encounters ischemia-reperfusion injury and recipient immune effectors immediately after implantation. Experimental and human studies demonstrate the dynamic coexistence and replacement of donor- and recipient-derived immune populations, with recipient cells acquiring phenotypes within the graft microenvironment. We distinguish transient donor-tissue activation from genuine tissue immune memory, which would require persistence of an exposure-induced molecular or functional state and an altered response to a subsequent challenge. Potential mechanisms include trained innate immunity, epigenetic and metabolic reprogramming, endothelial inflammatory memory, and persistent stromal-immune interactions. We propose that allograft biology be investigated at the level of the donor-recipient immune pair and outline longitudinal single-cell, spatial, and cell-of-origin approaches to test this concept in human heart transplantation.

articles.titulo: The Vaginal Microbiome-Mitochondria Axis: Implications for Genital Tract Infections.
articles.autores: Agoni L, Pericolini E, … De Seta F (5 autores)
articles.resumo_original: The vaginal microbiome influences epithelial and immune homeostasis through microbial metabolites, virulence factors, and other molecular signals, yet intracellular mechanisms translating microbial activity into host responses remain largely unexplored. Here, we propose the vaginal microbiome-mitochondria axis as a functional framework linking microbial activity to host-cell metabolism, redox signaling, immunity, and cell fate. We integrated evidence from vaginal microbiology, mitochondrial biology, mucosal immunology, and immunometabolism, distinguishing direct observations in the female genital tract from mechanistic evidence obtained in other host-microbe systems. Available evidence indicates that microbial products relevant to vaginal homeostasis and dysbiosis can modulate mitochondrial bioenergetics, reactive oxygen species generation and redox signaling, membrane potential, dynamics, and quality control pathways, while mitochondrial responses can influence epithelial integrity and antimicrobial and inflammatory functions. We further propose that the balance between mitochondrial adaptation and dysfunction may contribute to resolution or persistence of vaginal disorders and that incomplete mitochondrial recovery could contribute to an incomplete microbial ecosystem-host reset and recurrence. Although direct vaginal evidence remains limited, this framework identifies mitochondria as a potentially important functional interface between microbial ecology and host response and generates testable hypotheses for investigating whether mitochondrial homeostasis contributes to durable resolution of vaginal dysbiosis and infection.

articles.titulo: Redox signaling fidelity in immunosenescence and inflammaging: from oxidative stress to precision immune geroscience.
articles.autores: Lu W, Yan J
articles.resumo_original: Immunosenescence and inflammaging are accompanied by chronic inflammatory tone, impaired host-defense responses, defective resolution, and altered immunometabolic adaptation. Although these processes are often linked to oxidative stress, reactive oxygen species (ROS) also function as regulated immune signals. Here, we propose that aging immunity may involve not only increased oxidant burden but also a progressive loss of redox signaling fidelity, defined as the capacity of immune cells and tissues to generate, encode, transmit, decode, and resolve redox-dependent information with source specificity, spatially organized routing, temporal precision, biochemical reversibility, and proportionate downstream interpretation. We organize this framework into five information-flow layers: source-controlled reactive-species generation, reversible cysteine-centered and secondary-mediator encoding, spatially organized transmission, immune and inflammatory decoding, and resolution/reset by antioxidant, autophagy, mitophagy, lysosomal, and proteostatic systems. We then map age-associated fidelity loss onto T cells, B cells and hematopoietic progenitors, macrophages and microglia, neutrophils, dendritic cells, natural killer cells, regulatory T cells, and senescent-cell communication. The framework helps explain why related redox signals can support host defense, antigen-specific activation, and adaptive stress responses in one context, yet promote maladaptive NF-kappaB, NLRP3, cGAS-STING, interferon-linked inflammation, and senescence-associated secretory propagation when source coupling, timing, spatial routing, reversibility, decoder proportionality, or resolution fails. We also discuss why broad antioxidant suppression may underperform when it lowers oxidant abundance while flattening adaptive redox dynamics. Finally, we outline quantitative metrics, decisive experiments, controversies, and biomarker-guided therapeutic principles for precision immune geroscience.

articles.titulo: Nutrition, thyroid function, and tuberculosis: exploring the endocrine-immune axis.
articles.autores: Khachatourian N, Takhmazian R, Venketaraman V
articles.resumo_original: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major global health challenge, with undernutrition recognized as one of the most significant modifiable risk factors influencing disease susceptibility and clinical outcomes. Emerging evidence suggests that nutritional status may also affect TB risk indirectly through its impact on thyroid function and immune regulation. This review examines the current evidence linking nutrition, thyroid dysfunction, and susceptibility to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M. tuberculosis), with particular emphasis on the biological mechanisms that connect these factors. Essential micronutrients, including iodine, selenium, iron, zinc, and vitamin D, are critical for thyroid hormone synthesis, metabolism, antioxidant defense, and immune function. Deficiencies in these nutrients can impair thyroid physiology, disrupt endocrine homeostasis, and alter innate and adaptive immune responses that are essential for controlling M. tuberculosis infection. Thyroid hormones regulate macrophage activation, T-cell differentiation, cytokine production, immunometabolism, and oxidative stress, suggesting that thyroid dysfunction may compromise host resistance to TB. Conversely, chronic TB infection and antitubercular therapy may further disrupt thyroid function, creating a bidirectional relationship between these conditions. Collectively, the available evidence supports a conceptual framework in which nutritional deficiencies contribute to thyroid dysfunction, thyroid dysfunction impairs antimicrobial immunity, and TB further exacerbates nutritional and endocrine disturbances, establishing a self-perpetuating cycle that may increase disease susceptibility and worsen clinical outcomes. Although direct clinical evidence linking thyroid disorders with TB risk remains limited, the convergence of nutritional, endocrine, and immunological pathways provides a strong biological rationale for further investigation. Future prospective studies are needed to determine whether nutritional optimization, targeted micronutrient supplementation, and early identification and management of thyroid dysfunction can improve immune competence, reduce TB susceptibility, and enhance treatment outcomes in high-risk populations.

articles.titulo: Lipidomic Remodelling and Low Sperm Quality Associated with High-Fat Diet-Induced Gut Microbial Dysbiosis in Mice.
articles.autores: Pan M, Scarlata E, … O'Flaherty C (5 autores)
articles.resumo_original: Infertility affects one in six couples worldwide, with male infertility contributing to ~50% of cases. Rising obesity rates have been linked to impaired male fertility, potentially through alterations in the gut microbiota; however, underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. We characterized gut microbiome composition and lipidomic profiles in stool, serum, and testis samples. We assessed sperm quality in C57BL6 male mice fed a 45% fat diet (high-fat diet, HFD) or a 10% fat diet (normal diet, ND). We analyzed the gut microbiota by 16S rRNA sequencing. We measured short-chain fatty acids by gas chromatography. We performed untargeted lipidomic profiling of stool, serum, and testis using UPLC-MS/MS. CASA and cytochemical and immunocytochemical analyses assessed sperm quality and oxidative stress markers. HFD-fed mice exhibited gut microbiota dysbiosis characterized by an increased Bacillota/Bacteroidota ratio, altered bacterial community composition, increased acetic acid, and reduced butyric acid. Lipidomic analyses revealed distinct stool, serum, and testis lipid profiles, including increased abundance of gut microbiota-associated lipids containing odd-chain fatty acyl groups in HFD-fed mice. These alterations were accompanied by reduced sperm motility, impaired acrosomal integrity, epididymal sperm maturation and sperm capacitation, and elevated oxidative and nitrosative stress. Collectively, these findings support a gut-testis-epididymis axis in which altered gut microbiota-derived lipids contribute to oxidative stress and reduced sperm quality.

articles.titulo: Off-Target Effects of Recombinant Zoster Vaccine: Clinical Benefits, AS01B Adjuvant Immunobiology, and Observational Evidence.
articles.autores: Tang J, Balaji S, Oon HH
articles.resumo_original: Background/Objectives: The recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV), Shingrix®, has shown great efficacy in protecting against herpes zoster. However, emerging evidence suggests that this RZV might provide benefits that extend beyond preventing varicella zoster virus (VZV) reactivation. Specifically, this scoping review explored the literature to investigate the reported non-zoster, off-target effects of the Shingrix® RZV, and the possible mechanistic explanations for these effects. Methods: Keyword searches of PubMed database were conducted, along with manual searches of other relevant journals and reference lists of primary articles. Results: Evidence from the included studies demonstrated relationships between administration of RZV vaccination and reduced risk of dementia, Alzheimer's disease and major adverse cardiological events (MACEs), while also conferring geroprotective effects. Mechanistic studies identified two possible causes, namely VZV suppression and AS01B adjuvant immunoregulation. Prevention of herpes zoster resulted in reduced risk of associated cognitive impairment and vasculopathy, reducing incidence of dementia and MACE. AS01B adjuvant was also linked to persistent monocyte reprogramming, and enhanced innate immune response and memory, known as "trained immunity", which provided a plausible explanation for the observed off-target effects. Adverse events because of RZV administration were rare but included Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), autoimmune encephalitis and autoimmune flares occurring after vaccination. However, there is insufficient evidence to indicate a causal relationship between RZV administration and these rare immune-mediated adverse effects, and post-marketing surveillance still support a favourable safety profile. Conclusions: Current evidence suggests that RZV administration confers numerous off-target benefits via VZV suppression and the immunomodulatory effects of the AS01B adjuvant. As clinical evidence remains observational, further investigation of the pleiotropic effects of RZV should be carried out to explore its role in reducing all-cause mortality.

articles.titulo: Closing the Automation Gap in HPV-Based Cervical Cancer Screening: Independent External Validation of an AI Model for Dual-Stain Triage.
articles.autores: Lahrmann B, Keil A, … Grabe N (20 autores)
articles.resumo_original:
BACKGROUND: Primary human papillomavirus (HPV) screening has enabled scalable molecular detection in cervical cancer prevention, but downstream triage of HPV-positive individuals remains dependent on manual p16/Ki-67 dual-stain (DS) cytology interpretation.
